title: How to Make Better Decisions

reader_summary.headline: How do you make a smart and logical decision when you don't have all the facts, and probably never will?
reader_summary.overview: How do you make a smart and logical decision when you don't have all the facts, and probably never will? When and how do you decide to go against consensus opinion? And can you get better decision-making with practice?

key_points.text: Many founders, investors, and builders must make many critical decisions big and small every day.
key_points.evidence_quote: Many founders, investors, and builders must make many critical decisions big and small every day, and improving the quality of your decision-making process can become a big competitive advantage.

key_points.text: In this episode from October 2020, expert decision strategist, author, and professional poker player, Annie Duke, joins A16Z general partner Jeff Jordan.
key_points.evidence_quote: In this episode from October 2020, expert decision strategist, author, and professional poker player, Annie Duke, joins A16Z general partner Jeff Jordan, and they discuss some frameworks, strategies, and tactics for better decision-making by both individuals and organizations, in part based on Annie's second book, How to Decide.

key_points.text: This was Annie's second appearance on the podcast.
key_points.evidence_quote: This was Annie's second appearance on the podcast.

key_points.evidence_quote: She first joined A16Z co-founder, Mark and Driesen, and host Sonal to discuss her first book, Thinking in Betz, where she, Mark and Sonal talked about how to frame taking risks and placing bets, especially in the context of innovation.

thesis: The episode discusses frameworks and strategies for improving decision-making under uncertainty, focusing on separating decision quality from outcome quality. It highlights cognitive pitfalls like the paradox of experience, resulting, and hindsight bias, which cause individuals to learn bad lessons from single data points or reconstruct their past knowledge incorrectly after an outcome is known.
